analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for it by taxing earnings above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill to expand Social Security and add new taxes on high earnings was referred to the Finance Committee on April 16, 2018 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for every current and future beneficiary, use a cost-of-living formula that better matches what older Americans actually buy, and set a higher minimum benefit for people who worked many years at low wages. To pay for it, it would apply the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above $400,000 and slowly raise the payroll tax rate for all workers and employers over about 24 years. The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries. Every current and future beneficiary would get a modest across-the-board increase, because the bill raises the share of average earnings counted in the benefit formula from 90% to 93%. Beneficiaries would also get cost-of-living adjustments based on a new index tracking prices seniors actually face, which typically rises faster than the current index. People who worked at low wages for at least 11 years would get a new minimum benefit scaled up to 125% of the poverty line for those with 30 or more years of work. Beneficiaries earning under $50,000 (or $100,000 for couples) would stop paying federal income tax on their benefits, and any increased benefits would not count against eligibility for Medicaid, CHIP, or SSI.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security retirees and disability beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Raises the benefit formula so every beneficiary gets an increase, effective for benefits payable after December 2018 [S3].

Switches annual cost-of-living adjustments to a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish, because the current index tracks urban wage earners rather than retirees [S2] [S3].

Creates an alternative minimum benefit rising with years of work, reaching 125% of the poverty guideline for people with 30 or more years of work, so lifetime low earners are lifted above poverty [S3].
Raises the income thresholds before Social Security benefits become taxable to $50,000 for single filers and $100,000 for joint filers [S2] [S3].
Keeps any new benefit from counting as income for Medicaid, CHIP, and SSI eligibility so the increase does not cost low-income beneficiaries other assistance [S2] [S3].

Applies the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above $400,000 and counts those earnings in the benefit formula at a low 2% rate, closing a gap where earnings above the taxable maximum currently face no Social Security tax at all [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High earners and, over time, all workers and employers. Starting after 2018, earnings above $400,000 would be subject to the Social Security payroll tax and self-employment tax. Separately, the combined payroll tax rate would rise in small annual steps from 6.2% (employee side) to 7.4% by 2043, and the self-employment rate from 12.4% to 14.8%, paid by workers and employers in equal shares. Employers typically pass part of their payroll tax share to workers through lower wages.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, then gradually all workers and employers

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase falls on ordinary workers too: the employee rate climbs from 6.2% to 7.4% over roughly two decades, and employers pay a matching share that economists generally expect to show up partly as slower wage growth [S3].
Self-employed people would bear the full combined rate increase, from 12.4% to 14.8% over the same period [S3].

The bill does not include the CRS cost estimate or actuarial scoring in the record provided, so whether the added taxes fully finance the added benefits over 75 years cannot be verified from these sources [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and immediate for retirees, disabled workers, and low lifetime earners, while the cost is spread thinly: the tax on earnings above $400,000 falls only on the top slice of income, and the rate increase for everyone else is phased in a tenth of a percent at a time over 24 years. The main honest objection is that middle-income workers and their employers do share the gradual rate increase, and that the bill's long-term financing was never scored in the record provided. On the design as written, the gains to beneficiaries appear larger and more concentrated among lower-income seniors than the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and then nothing happened — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Blumenthal introduced the bill with Van Hollen on April 16, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
Two senators cosponsored the bill, both Democrats [S4].
The Senate Finance Committee took no further action on the bill, and the full action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social Security beneficiaries gained nothing, and the highest earners kept paying no Social Security tax on earnings above the roughly $128,000 taxable cap. The Senate Finance Committee and its chairman avoided a vote on raising payroll taxes and taxes on high earnings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and the Finance Committee's calendar

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act in the Senate on April 16, 2018.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.role: U.S. Senator from Maryland; original cosponsor

for.name: 2 of 47 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill without committee action.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats and no Republicans cosponsored; the bill then died in a Finance Committee chaired by a Republican, with no votes ever taken on it.

industries.note: For the first time, earnings above $400,000 would be subject to the Social Security payroll tax and self-employment tax, which currently stop applying above the annual taxable wage cap. That cost runs directly against the benefit increases ordinary beneficiaries would receive.
The employer share of the Social Security payroll tax would rise in steps from 6.2% to 7.4% by 2042. Employers typically shift part of that cost to workers through lower wages.

industries.industry: Self-employed workers and small business owners
industries.note: Self-employed people pay both halves of the tax, so their rate would climb from 12.4% to 14.8% over two decades — but self-employed retirees also receive the benefit increases.
